title: How to Spot a Lowball Offer
metaTitle: How to Spot a Lowball Mineral Rights Offer
metaDescription: The pressure tactics, number tricks, and paperwork shortcuts to watch for in Wyoming mineral rights offers, and what a fair one actually looks like.
heroLead: Every mineral owner eventually gets a letter or a cold call offering to buy. Some are legitimate. A few use the same handful of tactics to get a signature before an owner checks the number.
intro: Mail solicitations for mineral rights have picked up across Wyoming's producing counties over the past decade, and most of them are boilerplate letters sent to every owner on a county tax roll, without any specific knowledge of your interest.

That doesn't make every offer bad, but it means the number in that letter was generated without looking at your actual production history, and it's worth knowing what to check before you sign anything back.

sections.heading: The Pressure Tactics
paragraphs: A deadline attached to the offer, phrases like this expires in ten days, is the most common pressure tactic. Legitimate buyers doing real diligence on your interest generally don't need you to sign before they've even seen your statements.
Repeated calls pushing you toward a quick decision, or language suggesting the offer will drop if you wait, are both signs the buyer is working volume rather than valuing your specific tract.

Some letters lean on urgency around commodity prices, implying the window to sell is closing right now. Prices move constantly, in both directions, and that framing is more about getting a fast signature than reflecting anything true about timing.

sections.heading: The Number Tricks
paragraphs: A flat offer with no explanation of how it was calculated, no mention of your decimal interest, and no reference to your actual production, is usually a form letter number rather than a real appraisal of your specific interest.

Some letters advertise a price range in bold and then quote you the low end without explaining the gap, or lead with language implying you're getting a better deal than you'd get anywhere else, without showing any of the work behind that claim.

A few letters quote a number per net mineral acre without saying whether that figure reflects your county, your specific formation, or a much more active area entirely. A number without that context tells you almost nothing about your tract.

sections.heading: The Paperwork Shortcuts
paragraphs: Watch for a purchase agreement that doesn't clearly state the legal description of what's being bought, or one that bundles a broad power of attorney into the same document, which can grant far more authority than a simple mineral sale requires.

A legitimate buyer's paperwork should specify the exact tract, the decimal interest, and the purchase price in plain terms, and should give you time to have it reviewed before signing, not pressure to sign on the spot.

Watch also for a deed that conveys more than your letter describes, an all-inclusive clause sweeping in interests you didn't discuss. Read the deed itself, not only the cover letter, before signing anything.

sections.heading: What a Fair Offer Actually Looks Like
paragraphs: A fair offer is built from your actual deed, your production or lease history, and current activity in your county, and the buyer should be willing to explain how they arrived at the number if you ask.
It also gives you time. There's no reason a real buyer needs an answer in a week, and any pressure to skip reviewing the paperwork with someone you trust is itself a signal worth taking seriously.

A fair buyer will also tell you plainly if your interest doesn't fit what they buy, rather than pushing a number just to get a signature. That kind of straight answer is itself worth something when you're deciding who to trust with the sale.

faqs.question: Are all cold-mail mineral offers scams?
faqs.answer: No, most come from legitimate buyers casting a wide net, but the number is usually generic until they see your actual deed and statements. Treat the first letter as a starting point, not a final offer.

faqs.question: Should I be worried about a deadline on an offer?
faqs.answer: A short deadline pushing you to sign before reviewing the paperwork is a reasonable thing to push back on. A real buyer should be willing to extend it while you check the details.

faqs.question: What questions should I ask a buyer before accepting?
faqs.answer: Ask how they calculated the number, whether they've seen your recent statements, and what the purchase agreement includes beyond the sale price, including any power of attorney language.

faqs.question: Can I get a second opinion on an offer I've already received?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it's a reasonable step before signing. Comparing an unsolicited offer against one built from your actual production history often reveals whether the first number was fair.

faqs.question: What should a legitimate purchase agreement include?
faqs.answer: The exact legal description of the tract, your decimal interest, the purchase price, and clear terms without bundling in broad authority beyond the mineral sale itself.

faqs.question: Is it normal to get several offers from different buyers?
faqs.answer: Yes, especially in active counties. Comparing more than one offer is a reasonable way to gauge whether a specific number reflects your interest fairly.

faqs.question: Should I be suspicious of an offer with no phone number to call?
faqs.answer: Yes. A legitimate buyer should be reachable directly by phone to answer questions before you sign anything, rather than only through a return mail address.
